claims.evidence: The manuscript infers this from their ribosome stalling data and cites related studies.

claims.claim: Stop-codon readthrough has been reported to be more frequent in neurons than in other cell types.
claims.source: Stop-codon readthrough has been reported to be more frequent in neurons than in other cell types (Hudson et al., 2021; Karki et al., 2022; Prieto-Godino et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on stop-codon readthrough.

claims.claim: Readthrough events extend the protein C-terminus.
claims.source: Because the readthrough events extend the protein C-terminus, its regulation can add yet another layer of cell-type diversity (Dunn et al., 2013; Jungreis et al., 2011; Klagges et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge and cites supporting studies.

claims.claim: Neurons allocate more ribosomes to proteins related to neurotransmission, visual sensing, and oxidative phosphorylation.
claims.source: Neurons allocate more ribosomes to proteins related to neurotransmission, visual sensing, and oxidative phosphorylation, while glial cells synthesize transporters and enzymes for metabolism of amino acid, fatty acid, or carbohydrates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports ribosome allocation patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claims.claim: Glial cells synthesize transporters and enzymes for metabolism of amino acid, fatty acid, or carbohydrates.
claims.source: Neurons allocate more ribosomes to proteins related to neurotransmission, visual sensing, and oxidative phosphorylation, while glial cells synthesize transporters and enzymes for metabolism of amino acid, fatty acid, or carbohydrates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports protein synthesis patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claims.claim: A significant amount of neuronal and glial cells has a common developmental origin from neuro-glioblasts.
claims.source: Despite these clear differences and specialization, a significant amount of neuronal and glial cells has a common developmental origin. They originate from a stem cell lineage known as neuro-glioblasts (Lai and Lee, 2006; Viktorin et al., 2011), and the fate of these cells can be altered by the expression of a single gene, glial cells missing (gcm) (Hartenstein, 2011; Hosoya et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on developmental origins.

claims.claim: The fate of neuro-glioblast cells can be altered by the expression of a single gene, glial cells missing (gcm).
claims.source: They originate from a stem cell lineage known as neuro-glioblasts (Lai and Lee, 2006; Viktorin et al., 2011), and the fate of these cells can be altered by the expression of a single gene, glial cells missing (gcm) (Hartenstein, 2011; Hosoya et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on cell fate determination.

claims.claim: Translational regulations may play a particularly important role in neuronal and glial sister cell types with distinct physiological roles.
claims.source: Therefore, translational regulations, in addition to transcriptional diversity, may play a particularly important role in these sister cell types with distinct physiological roles.
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers this from their data on translational regulation and cited developmental biology.

claims.claim: In the Drosophila brain, approximately 100 stem cell lineages diverge into more than 5000 morphologically distinct cell types.
claims.source: In the Drosophila brain, approximately 100 stem cell lineages diverge into more than 5000 morphologically distinct cell types (Ito et al., 2013; Scheffer et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on Drosophila brain cell diversity.

claims.claim: Translational regulations may play significant roles in differentiating neuronal or glial subtypes.
claims.source: Hence, translational regulations similar to those described in this study, or other possible regulations, may play significant roles in further differentiating neuronal or glial subtypes.
claims.evidence: The manuscript speculates about broader implications of their findings.

claims.claim: The UAS-Rh1-Venus reporter showed heterogeneous expression even among neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, our UAS-Rh1-Venus reporter showed heterogeneous expression even among neurons, contrasting with the more uniform expression observed in the control UASz-GFP reporter (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports observed expression patterns from imaging data.

claims.claim: ChAT and VAChT are transcribed in many glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons but their protein synthesis is inhibited.
claims.source: In accordance, choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), an enzyme needed to synthesize acetylcholine, and vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) are transcribed in many glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons but its protein synthesis is inhibited (Chen et al., 2023; Lacin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing this pattern.

claims.claim: Substantial post-transcriptional regulations are implicated during development.
claims.source: Substantial post-transcriptional regulations are also implicated during development (Li et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on developmental regulation.

claims.claim: Multiple layers of transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulations shape the proteome diversity of cell types in the nervous system.
claims.source: Taken together, multiple layers of transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulations should shape the proteome diversity of cell types in the nervous system.
claims.evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from their data and cited literature.

claims.claim: Cell-type-specific Ribo-seq and RNA-seq based on immunoprecipitation of genetically tagged RpL3 could contain biases such as underestimation of mRNA level with little or no translational activity.
claims.source: Because our cell-type-specific Ribo-seq and RNA-seq are based on immunoprecipitation of genetically tagged RpL3 (Chen and Dickman, 2017), the read counts could contain biases, such as underestimation of mRNA level with little or no translational activity, or over- and under-representation of certain cell types originating from the heterogeneous expression of the drivers.
claims.evidence: The manuscript acknowledges potential limitations of their methodology.

claims.claim: Cell-type-specific Ribo-seq and RNA-seq could contain over- and under-representation of certain cell types originating from the heterogeneous expression of the drivers.
claims.source: Because our cell-type-specific Ribo-seq and RNA-seq are based on immunoprecipitation of genetically tagged RpL3 (Chen and Dickman, 2017), the read counts could contain biases, such as underestimation of mRNA level with little or no translational activity, or over- and under-representation of certain cell types originating from the heterogeneous expression of the drivers.
claims.evidence: The manuscript acknowledges potential limitations of their methodology.

results.result: Ribosome profiling in Drosophila heads successfully captured translation with 96.2% of footprints mapping to coding sequences and displaying characteristic 3-nt periodicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 report standard quality control metrics for Ribo-seq experiments. The high percentage of CDS mapping and 3-nt periodicity are expected hallmarks of successful ribosome profiling, supported by Figure 1B showing the periodicity pattern.

results.result: Transcriptome and translatome show moderate correlation (R²=0.664) with substantial variability in translational efficiency across genes, exemplified by Trehalase showing much higher TE than Shaker despite similar transcript levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C8-C9 collectively demonstrate post-transcriptional regulation through correlation analysis and specific examples. The R² value, genome-wide TE variability (>20-fold), and the Sh/Treh comparison provide converging evidence for translational regulation.

results.result: KEGG pathway analysis reveals that transcripts for fatty acid metabolism and proteasome show high TE, while neuronal genes including ion channels, GPCRs, and ribosomal proteins show low TE, suggesting translational suppression of neuronal transcripts in whole heads.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 report KEGG enrichment analysis results from whole-head Ribo-seq data. The findings are internally consistent and supported by Figure 1H-I, though the interpretation of 'translational suppression' for neuronal genes in whole heads may reflect tissue composition rather than active suppression.

results.result: The UAS-RpL3::FLAG construct on the third chromosome shows minimal leakage expression, no morphological defects, and subcellular localization consistent with endogenous ribosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 validate the technical approach for cell-type-specific ribosome profiling. Immunohistochemistry data (Figure 2A, supplements) confirm proper expression and localization of the tagged ribosomal protein, establishing the validity of the experimental system.

results.result: Cell-type-specific Ribo-seq successfully profiled translatomes from neurons and glia with high reproducibility (R²>0.9), detecting footprints on ~78-80% of annotated genes, with strong enrichment of cell-type markers and depletion of non-target markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C24 establish the quality and specificity of cell-type-specific Ribo-seq. High reproducibility, appropriate marker enrichment/depletion, and KEGG pathway enrichment (Figure 2B, supplements) validate the immunoprecipitation approach for isolating cell-type-specific translatomes.

results.result: Neurons show greater protein synthesis of oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial ribosome proteins while glia show higher expression of glycolysis proteins, supporting the glia-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 report differential metabolic protein synthesis between cell types. The KEGG analysis results are consistent with known metabolic specialization, though the support for the lactate shuttle hypothesis is inferential rather than direct experimental validation.

results.result: Ribosome footprints detected on Hsr-ω, previously annotated as a long non-coding RNA, suggest synthesis of undescribed polypeptides.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 report an interesting observation of ribosome footprints on a lncRNA. While the footprints are detected (C28), the inference of polypeptide synthesis (C29) requires additional validation such as mass spectrometry or functional studies to confirm translation products.

results.result: Fatty acid metabolism genes show lower TE in neurons and glia compared to whole heads, suggesting selective translational enhancement in fat bodies where these genes are highly expressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 integrate cell-type-specific TE data with published tissue expression data. The comparative analysis across whole head, neurons, and glia, combined with cited fat body expression data, supports the inference of tissue-specific translational regulation.

results.result: Genes involved in neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction show significantly higher TE in neurons but lower in glia, with weak TE correlation between cell types (R²=0.534). Neuronal genes including ion channels, GPCRs, neuropeptides, and visual perception proteins show particularly low TE in glia, with cell-type distinctions more pronounced at the translational than transcriptional level.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 collectively demonstrate cell-type-specific translational regulation. The weak TE correlation (C35), genome-wide trends (C36), specific gene categories (C37), and comparison to transcriptional differences (C38-C39) provide strong converging evidence that translation substantially enhances cell-type distinctions.

results.result: Fat-body-related genes show lower TE in neurons with remarkable ribosomal accumulation at start codons specifically in neurons; these mRNAs are highly abundant in fat bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 identify a specific pattern of ribosome stalling at initiation codons for fat body genes in neurons. The observation is supported by Ribo-seq data and reanalysis of published tissue expression data, suggesting translational control at the initiation-to-elongation transition.

results.result: Glial ribosome footprints on differentially translated transcripts (DTTs) suppressed in glia show remarkable bias toward 5' leaders, commonly observed on neuronal genes like Rab3, Syt4, Arr1, and Syn, suggesting that translation of 5' leaders differentiates protein synthesis among cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 identify a key mechanism of cell-type-specific translational regulation. The 5' leader bias is specific to DTTs (C44-C45), observed across multiple neuronal genes (C46), and shows reciprocal patterns for glial genes in neurons (C47), supporting the proposed mechanism (C48).

results.result: Metagene analysis reveals strong ribosome accumulation on upstream AUG codons and near-cognate codons in 5' leaders but not within CDS. Neuronal transcripts typically contain long 5' leaders with many upstream AUGs, leading to the proposal that glia suppress neuronal transcript translation via uORF-mediated ribosome stalling.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 provide mechanistic insight into 5' leader-mediated regulation. The metagene analysis (C49-C51), structural features of neuronal transcripts (C52), and integration of these observations support the uORF-mediated suppression model (C53), though direct causation requires experimental validation.

results.result: Rh1 shows active translation almost exclusively in neurons, with ribosome footprints heavily biased to 5' leader in glia and striking accumulation on putative uORFs composed of start and stop codons.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C56-C57 characterize Rh1 as a specific example of the general pattern. The Ribo-seq data showing cell-type-specific translation and 5' leader accumulation in glia are consistent with the proposed uORF-mediated regulation mechanism.

results.result: Transgenic reporter experiments with Rh1 UTR sequences show that while reporter mRNA is detected in both neurons and glia, protein levels are strikingly weak in glia. Mutation of six-base putative uORFs significantly increases protein-to-mRNA ratio in glia but not neurons, demonstrating that small uORFs in the 5' leader confer selective translational suppression in glia.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 provide direct experimental validation of the uORF-mediated suppression mechanism. The reporter experiments with wild-type and mutant constructs, combined with quantification of protein-to-mRNA ratios, establish causality for uORF function in cell-type-specific translational control.

results.result: Translational efficiency of neuronal proteins including ion channels and neurotransmitter receptors is maintained low in glia with ribosome footprints biased toward 5' leaders, leading to preferential translation in neurons and enhancing cell-type distinction in the nervous system.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 synthesize the main findings into the central conclusion. The comprehensive Ribo-seq data, mechanistic insights from uORF analysis, and experimental validation with reporters collectively support that translational regulation enhances cell-type distinctions.

results.result: Long 5' leaders with numerous uORFs are observed in mammalian neuronal transcripts, and 5' leader-mediated translational regulation is known to be critical for environmental stress responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 cite prior literature to contextualize the findings. These are well-established observations from previous studies that provide evolutionary and functional context for the mechanisms described in this work.

results.result: Translation initiation factors eIF1, eIF2α kinases, and DENR/MCT1 that facilitate translation of uORF-containing transcripts are expressed more in neurons than glia, potentially underlying cell-type-specific translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 report established knowledge and expression data, but C72 is speculative. While the differential expression of these factors is interesting and consistent with the model, direct functional evidence linking their activity to the observed cell-type-specific translation is lacking.

results.result: Transition from initiation to elongation may serve as a regulatory checkpoint enhancing cell-type distinctions.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by the ribosome stalling data at start codons (C42) and cited literature. The observation of initiation-elongation transition control in fat body genes provides evidence for this regulatory checkpoint, though more extensive validation would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Neurons allocate more ribosomes to neurotransmission, visual sensing, and oxidative phosphorylation proteins, while glia synthesize transporters and metabolic enzymes for amino acid, fatty acid, and carbohydrate metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 summarize cell-type-specific protein synthesis patterns from Ribo-seq data. These findings are consistent with known functional specializations of neurons and glia and are supported by the KEGG pathway analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Neuronal and glial cells share common developmental origins from neuro-glioblasts, with cell fate alterable by single gene expression (gcm), suggesting translational regulation plays important roles in differentiating these sister cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 cite established developmental biology, while C80 makes a reasonable inference. The shared developmental origin combined with the demonstrated translational differences supports the interpretation that translational regulation contributes to cell-type specification beyond transcriptional control.

results.result: Translational regulation may differentiate neuronal and glial subtypes, consistent with heterogeneous UAS-Rh1-Venus reporter expression among neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is speculative about subtype differentiation, while C83 reports observed heterogeneity. The reporter heterogeneity (C83) is suggestive but insufficient to establish that translational regulation differentiates subtypes without more detailed subtype-specific analysis.

results.result: Multiple layers of transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation shape proteome diversity of cell types in the nervous system.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 synthesizes the overall findings with cited literature. The comprehensive Ribo-seq and RNA-seq data demonstrating translational regulation, combined with cited examples of other post-transcriptional mechanisms, support this integrative conclusion.

results.result: The cell-type-specific Ribo-seq and RNA-seq approach based on immunoprecipitation of tagged RpL3 may contain biases including underestimation of mRNAs with little translation and over/under-representation of cell types due to heterogeneous driver expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 acknowledge methodological limitations. These are valid concerns inherent to the TRAP-based approach, and the authors appropriately recognize potential biases that could affect quantitative interpretations of their data.

results.result: The authors report that 96.2% of ribosome footprints mapped to annotated CDS with clear 3-nt periodicity, demonstrating the quality of their whole-head Ribo-seq data.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the sequencing datasets and bioinformatic analyses as 'robust and reliable' with no specific concerns raised about the basic quality metrics of the Ribo-seq data. The periodicity and CDS mapping are standard quality control measures that reviewers implicitly accept.

results.result: The authors demonstrate substantial post-transcriptional regulation in whole heads, showing imperfect correlation between transcript levels and ribosome footprints (R²=0.664), with specific examples like Shaker and Trehalase having similar transcript levels but different ribosome occupancy, and genome-wide TE variability exceeding 20-fold.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these findings as establishing the presence of post-transcriptional regulation. One reviewer notes 'it is well established that there is extensive post-transcriptional gene regulation in nervous systems' and accepts the data showing differential TE. No concerns are raised about these basic observations.

results.result: KEGG pathway analysis of whole-head data revealed that transcripts for fatty acid metabolism and proteasome are actively translated, while ribosome proteins and neuronal ligand-receptor interaction genes show low TE, suggesting translational suppression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these pathway enrichment findings without specific critique. The data are presented as part of the initial characterization of translational regulation in whole heads, and reviewers describe the overall findings as logically presented with clear data depiction.

results.result: The UAS-RpL3::FLAG construct on the third chromosome showed minimal leakage expression, no morphological defects, and localization consistent with endogenous ribosomes (concentrated in cell bodies but detectable in neurites).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises significant concerns about the RpL3::FLAG system, noting 'substantial cell-to-cell variation in RpL3::FLAG expression' and questioning whether this 'may cause certain neuronal/glial types to be overrepresented in their datasets.' The reviewer also notes the authors 'do not discuss whether RpL3::FLAG only present in the cell body or if it is also trafficked to the neuronal/glial processes where localized translation is known to occur.'

results.result: Cell-type-specific Ribo-seq successfully profiled translatomes from neurons (10,821 genes, 78.4%) and glia (10,994 genes, 79.7%) with high reproducibility (R²>0.9) and strong enrichment of FLAG-tagged RpL3 (7.8-fold in neurons, 42.7-fold in glia).
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the sequencing datasets as 'robust and reliable' with 'decent reproducibility.' While concerns are raised about potential biases in the method (see C87-88), the basic technical success and reproducibility of the cell-type-specific profiling are accepted.

results.result: Cell-type-specific Ribo-seq showed strong enrichment of known marker genes and depletion of non-target markers, with KEGG analysis confirming enrichment of footprints on genes associated with known cell-type functions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge that the authors 'demonstrate the specificity of their cell-type-based ribosome profiling: known glial mRNAs are efficiently translated in glia and likewise in neurons as well.' This validation is accepted without specific critique.

results.result: Neurons show greater protein synthesis related to oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial ribosome proteins, while glia show higher expression of glycolysis-associated proteins, supporting the glia-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis.
results.evaluation: These metabolic specialization findings are presented as part of the cell-type characterization and are not specifically challenged by reviewers. The data are accepted as part of the broader demonstration of cell-type-specific translation patterns.

results.result: Clustered ribosome footprints were detected on Hsr-ω, previously annotated as a long non-coding RNA, strongly suggesting synthesis of undescribed polypeptides.
results.evaluation: This finding is presented as an additional observation from the Ribo-seq data and is not challenged by reviewers. It represents a secondary discovery from the profiling experiments.

results.result: Fatty acid metabolism genes showed lower TE in neurons and glia compared to whole head, with remarkable ribosomal accumulation on start codons in neurons; these genes are highly expressed in fat bodies, suggesting selective translational enhancement in fat body tissue.
results.evaluation: These findings are presented as examples of tissue-specific translational regulation and are not specifically challenged by reviewers. They serve as supporting evidence for differential TE across tissues.

results.result: Genes involved in neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction show significantly higher TE in neurons but lower in glia, with weak TE correlation between cell types (R²=0.534). Many neuronal genes (ion channels, GPCRs, neuropeptides, visual perception proteins) show particularly low TE in glia, with distinctions more exaggerated at translation than transcription level, indicating substantial contributions of translational regulation to cell-type-specific protein expression.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept that differential TE exists, Reviewer 3 raises a fundamental concern: 'it is still rather unclear whether this mechanism would have any significant impact on differential gene expression between cell types in vivo. Considering that it's mostly occurring on genes that are already strongly differentially transcribed, that doesn't appear very likely.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'overinterpret their data by claiming that such suppression is key for maintaining glial/neuronal identity...but do not present any evidence that loss of such regulation has any impact on cellular identity.' This challenges the functional significance claim (C40).

results.result: Glial ribosome footprints on differentially translated transcripts (DTTs) suppressed in glia were remarkably biased toward 5' leaders, commonly observed on neuronal genes (Rab3, Syt4, Arr1, Syn), while glial marker genes showed accumulated footprints in 5' leaders specifically in neurons, suggesting that translation of 5' leaders in selective mRNAs differentiates protein synthesis among cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises critical methodological concerns: 'they show no evidence that glial mRNAs...present a different pattern, say that of higher ribosome occupancy in CDS vs. 5' leaders. This type of a positive control is a glaring omission from many of their analyses.' Additionally, Reviewer 2 notes that 'cycloheximide...and many other translation inhibitors, are known to non-uniformly bias reads towards start codons' and this 'important caveat and its implications on the start-codon occupancy analysis...are not acknowledged.'

results.result: Metagene analysis revealed strong accumulation of footprints on upstream AUG codons and near-cognate codons (NUG/AUN) in 5' leaders, but not within CDS. Neuronal transcripts typically contain long 5' leaders with many upstream AUGs, leading to the proposal that glia suppress neuronal transcript translation by stalling ribosomes on 5' leaders via uORF.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically challenges this analysis: 'Cycloheximide, and many other translation inhibitors, are known to non-uniformly bias reads towards start codons...This important caveat and its implications on the start-codon occupancy analysis in Fig. 4 are not acknowledged.' The reviewer suggests 'the ideal resolution would be ribosome profiling data set from 40S footprinting or harringtonine-treated samples...to show true accumulation of ribosomes at AUG codons.' This raises significant doubt about whether the observed accumulation represents true biological stalling or methodological artifact.

results.result: Rh1 (Rhodopsin 1), which encodes an opsin detecting multiple sensory modalities, shows active translation almost exclusively in neurons, with ribosome footprints heavily biased to 5' leader in glia and striking accumulation on putative uORFs composed only of start and stop codons.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 questions the choice of Rh1: 'given that the neuron data are from all nsyb-positive cells but that Rh1 is expressed only in R1-R6 photoreceptors, it is unclear what motivated them to chose Rh1 as opposed to an mRNA that is more broadly expressed in neurons.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Rh1, for instance, is not just differentially expressed between neurons and glia, but it is actually only expressed by a very specific neuronal type (photoreceptors). Thus it's not clear to me why the glia would need this 5' stalling mechanism to fully suppress Rh1 expression, while all the other neurons can apparently do so without it.'

results.result: Using a transgenic Rh1-UTR reporter driven by Tub-GAL4, the authors show that reporter mRNA was detected in both neurons and glia, but protein levels were heterogeneous and weak in glia. When putative uORFs were mutated, the protein-to-mRNA ratio significantly increased in glia but not neurons, providing evidence that small upstream ORFs in the 5' leader confer selective translational suppression in glia.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises multiple concerns about this experiment: 'Similar to the heterogeneity in nsyb- and repo-GAL4 expression...Fig. 5C shows substantial variation in the expression of the UAS-GFP reporter driven by tub-GAL4. This variable GAL4 activity makes the mRNA abundance data difficult to interpret.' The reviewer also notes 'the lack of a cellular compartment marker...makes it impossible to determine which cell the mRNA signal is in' and 'there are also no negative controls...presented for the mRNA probes.' Reviewer 3 finds the image 'rather unconvincing' and notes 'there are no quantifications of colocalization, or even sample size information provided.' Post-revision, Reviewer 2 states the authors 'satisfactorily addressed most of my concerns,' suggesting improvements were made.

results.result: The main conclusion that translational efficiency of neuronal proteins (ion channels, neurotransmitter receptors) is maintained low in glia through ribosome stalling on 5' leaders, and that translational regulation enhances distinction of cell types in the nervous system.
results.evaluation: The Editor states 'the evidence supporting the model is solid, although only one example...is studied in detail.' However, Reviewer 2 notes 'they overinterpret their data by claiming that such suppression is key for maintaining glial/neuronal identity...but do not present any evidence that loss of such regulation has any impact on cellular identity.' Post-revision, Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'while their data beautifully show that there is differential regulation of transcripts across neurons and glia, they do not provide evidence that such regulation is required for cell identity.' Reviewer 3 states 'it is still rather unclear whether this mechanism would have any significant impact on differential gene expression between cell types in vivo.'

results.result: The authors acknowledge that their cell-type-specific Ribo-seq and RNA-seq method based on immunoprecipitation of tagged RpL3 could contain biases, including underestimation of mRNAs with little translational activity and over/under-representation of certain cell types due to heterogeneous driver expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly raises these concerns, stating the authors 'do not acknowledge possible biases in their analytical methods' and noting that 'there are mRNAs on which the full ribosome moiety does not assemble and these are effectively excluded from this data set. Ideally, a more complete picture of the mRNA landscape can be obtained by 40S subunit profiling but I appreciate that this is technically very challenging. At minimum, this caveat needs to be acknowledged.' The manuscript text shows the authors did acknowledge these limitations.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate C1-C2 (Ribo-seq quality metrics) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval explicitly notes the high CDS mapping and 3-nt periodicity as expected hallmarks, while peer reviewers describe the datasets as 'robust and reliable' with implicit acceptance of these quality control measures.

Both evaluate C3-C5, C8-C9 (post-transcriptional regulation evidence) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes converging evidence from correlation analysis and specific examples, while peer reviewers acknowledge these findings establish post-transcriptional regulation and note it is 'well established' in nervous systems.

Both evaluate C10-C13 (KEGG enrichment in whole heads) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes internal consistency but questions interpretation of 'translational suppression' as potentially reflecting tissue composition, while peer reviewers accept the pathway enrichment findings without specific critique.

OpenEval evaluates C14-C17 (RpL3::FLAG validation) as SUPPORTED based on immunohistochemistry confirming proper expression and localization. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising significant concerns about 'substantial cell-to-cell variation' in expression and potential overrepresentation of certain cell types, plus questions about subcellular localization.

Both evaluate C18-C22 (cell-type-specific Ribo-seq quality and reproducibility) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes high reproducibility and marker enrichment/depletion, while peer reviewers describe datasets as 'robust and reliable' with 'decent reproducibility,' though noting potential biases in the method.

Both address cell-type-specific profiling validation. OpenEval's R5 covers broader quality metrics (C18-C24) rated SUPPORTED, while peer R6 specifically addresses marker specificity (C23-C24) as SUPPORTED, acknowledging the demonstration of known glial/neuronal mRNAs being efficiently translated in appropriate cell types.

Both evaluate C25-C27 (differential metabolic protein synthesis) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes consistency with known metabolic specialization but identifies the lactate shuttle support as inferential, while peer reviewers accept these findings as part of cell-type characterization without specific challenge.

OpenEval evaluates C28-C29 (lncRNA translation) as UNCERTAIN, noting that while footprints are detected, polypeptide synthesis inference requires additional validation. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting this as a secondary discovery without challenge.

Both address tissue-specific translational regulation. OpenEval's R8 covers C30-C32 rated SUPPORTED, while peer R9 covers C30-C32 plus C41-C43 also rated SUPPORTED. Both accept these as examples of differential TE across tissues without specific challenge.

OpenEval's R10 addresses C41-C43 (ribosome stalling at initiation codons for fat body genes) rated SUPPORTED. Peer R9 includes these claims along with C30-C32, also rated SUPPORTED, accepting them as evidence for tissue-specific translational regulation.

OpenEval evaluates C33-C40 (cell-type-specific translational regulation) as SUPPORTED with strong converging evidence. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with fundamental concerns about functional significance: whether the mechanism has 'any significant impact on differential gene expression' in vivo, especially since it occurs on already differentially transcribed genes, and noting lack of evidence that loss of regulation impacts cellular identity.

OpenEval evaluates C44-C48 (5' leader bias mechanism) as SUPPORTED based on DTT-specific patterns and reciprocal observations. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising critical methodological concerns about lack of positive controls (glial mRNAs showing different patterns) and cycloheximide-induced bias toward start codons, which is not acknowledged.

OpenEval evaluates C49-C53 (uORF-mediated regulation) as SUPPORTED though noting direct causation requires validation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, specifically challenging the analysis due to cycloheximide bias toward start codons and suggesting the observed accumulation may be methodological artifact rather than true biological stalling, recommending 40S footprinting or harringtonine-treated samples.

OpenEval evaluates C54, C56-C57 (Rh1 as specific example) as SUPPORTED, consistent with proposed uORF mechanism. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning why Rh1 was chosen given it's only expressed in R1-R6 photoreceptors while neuron data are from all nsyb-positive cells, and questioning why glia would need 5' stalling to suppress Rh1 when other neurons apparently suppress it without this mechanism.

OpenEval evaluates C58-C62 (reporter validation experiments) as SUPPORTED, stating they establish causality for uORF function. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about variable GAL4 activity making mRNA data difficult to interpret, lack of cellular compartment markers, no negative controls for mRNA probes, unconvincing images, and no quantifications or sample size information. Post-revision, concerns were largely addressed.

OpenEval evaluates C63-C65 (main conclusions) as SUPPORTED by comprehensive data and validation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with Editor noting evidence is 'solid' but only one example studied in detail. Reviewers note lack of evidence that loss of regulation impacts cellular identity and question whether the mechanism has significant impact in vivo, especially since it occurs on already differentially transcribed genes.

Both evaluate C87-C88 (methodological limitations acknowledgment) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these are valid concerns inherent to TRAP-based approaches that authors appropriately recognize. Peer reviewers explicitly raised these concerns, noting exclusion of mRNAs without full ribosome assembly and requesting acknowledgment of these caveats, which the manuscript text shows was done.

OpenEval evaluates C66-C67 (prior literature context) as SUPPORTED, noting these cite well-established observations providing evolutionary and functional context. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluates C70-C72 (translation initiation factors) as UNCERTAIN, noting C72 is speculative without direct functional evidence linking factor activity to observed cell-type-specific translation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluates C73 (initiation-elongation transition control) as SUPPORTED by ribosome stalling data and cited literature, though noting more validation would strengthen the conclusion. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
